text: The pull runs three ways at once: a household, a congregation, and one person he was never meant to want. Jayro Bustamante gives his central figure everything a man of standing is supposed to have, a wife and children and a place among believers, so that the choice in front of him costs all of it or nothing at all. That is the hard arithmetic of Temblores, and the film declines to soften it by supplying a villain. The people applying the pressure are the people who love him; the language is care and the instrument is faith. A hundred and seven minutes in Spanish, and the strain is less about being discovered than about being loved into agreement. It circulates among viewers who follow Bustamante's other work, which fits how it plays: not an argument aimed at strangers, but a case observed close enough to hurt.

The letters come first: a student known only as L writes to a lover who is away, while around her a government answers student protest with force. Payal Kapadia files this as documentary, which is the decision worth sitting with, since the record of what happened on Indian campuses reaches us through a private correspondence rather than around it, addressed to one absent man instead of to a public. Ninety-nine minutes, in Hindi, and the two registers will not stay apart: a man who has gone quiet, a country closing a door, one voice reporting both. Its audience so far is made of people who came through Kapadia's other films. What they find here is the method with its cover off, intimacy working as the instrument of witness rather than as relief from it.

Two hundred and twenty-eight minutes, one building, fifty men. Wang Bing filmed inside a psychiatric institution in Yunnan whose residents were placed there for killing someone, for offending an official, or for having been born with a disability the state had nowhere else to put. The length is the argument. Past a certain duration a viewer stops waiting for the film to deliver a case and begins to notice the building instead: the shape of a day with nothing in it that has to be done, and how much of institutional life turns out to be waiting inside that shape. Nobody is diagnosed here, since diagnosis would require an authority standing outside the ward, and none is admitted. It asks for the better part of an afternoon and returns confinement as weather rather than as event.

An eye that will not close, not even in sleep, belongs to the man Roy and Gilbert pick up on their fishing trip. It converts an ordinary problem, two against one, wait until he dozes, run, into seventy-one minutes of arithmetic that never comes out. Ida Lupino keeps the apparatus small: a car, a road, three men, and a stretch of country where help is theoretical. The economy is not modesty. At this length nothing can be spent on relief, and the pressure lands where it belongs, on two ordinary friends told in advance that they are useful for now. It sits in the National Film Registry, company usually kept by larger pictures. This one gets there on a single physical fact and the nerve to build a thriller around a face that cannot be read.

A man and a dog go up a mountain, and seventy-eight minutes are asked to carry a full cycle of seasons and the span of a single day at the same time. That is a demand no plot could meet, and no plot is offered. The catalogue files Stan Brakhage's film under fantasy, and the label sits better than documentary would: the climb is real labour, and what the film does to it belongs to the region where images stop reporting and begin behaving. It is close to unquotable. There is no scene to describe to a friend afterwards, only the memory of pictures arriving faster than the habit of reading pictures can keep up with them. The National Film Registry keeps it alongside works with casts and dialogue. Seventy-eight minutes is a long time at that pitch of attention, and the duration is the work rather than an obstacle to it.

A kitchen table in a Brussels apartment, and a laptop somewhere nearby so the conversation can continue when the daughter is in Oklahoma. Chantal Akerman filmed her mother Natalia, born in Poland and long settled in Belgium, eating and talking and remembering, sometimes with Chantal's sister Sylvaine in the room. A hundred and thirteen minutes of that, and the questions a documentary usually puts to its subject go unasked. What accumulates instead is duration: how long a meal takes, how much of a life gets mentioned in passing and then left, how a video call keeps a voice while flattening it. TSPDT lists it among the thousand greatest films, an odd berth for a picture shot mostly at one table. An old woman deciding what she will and will not say is the event, and the camera's refusal to hurry her is the method.

The Academy Award it took home was for editing, which is the right prize for a film that is mostly preparation. A hundred and seventy-three minutes about an escape means the bulk of the running time goes to the getting ready, and getting ready has no rhythm of its own; it is a hundred small jobs proceeding at once, on a schedule nobody is permitted to write down. Cutting is what turns that into suspense. John Sturges also has the camp's own logic to work with: the Nazis gathered their most persistent Allied escapers into one high-security place and thereby assembled a workforce. Based on a true story, and it shows in the scheduling rather than the heroics. Most people have seen this one, or believe they have. What surprises on a return is how long it stays with the preparation before anyone reaches open ground.

A film can sit at 5.3 with a hundred and fifty thousand voters and still hold a place on the BBC's hundred best of the century; this is the one that does. Four students rob a restaurant to pay for a week of spring break in Florida, and the week hands them a man with his own use for them. Harmony Korine spends ninety-four minutes refusing to separate the holiday from the felony, so the footage that sells the trip is the footage that prosecutes it, and no comfortable seat is provided from which to disapprove. The catalogue files it as drama and crime, and neither label gets to win. The ratings are recording that discomfort rather than a verdict on craft. What is actually in dispute is whether an image can criticise a pleasure while delivering it at full strength, and the answer shifts depending on the hour it is watched.

A coffee salesman sets out believing that diligence gets rewarded, and Britain spends three hours testing the proposition. Lindsay Anderson gives him a sample case and a route, then arranges the improbable and the ironic in his path until his optimism starts to look like a raw material other people are working with. The catalogue files the picture under comedy, music, fantasy and drama at once, which reads less like indecision than like fair warning: the picaresque licenses Anderson to break register whenever a scene has finished its business, and he takes the licence often. At a hundred and eighty-four minutes the joke has to keep renewing itself, and the nerve of the thing is that the punchline never changes. Britain in 1973, described by someone who has stopped expecting it to improve.

A 1931 jungle melodrama went into the hands of a man who kept only its leading actress, and came back out twenty minutes long. Joseph Cornell cut East of Borneo down to Rose Hobart herself, and the effect of the subtraction is not tribute but unease: with the plot machinery gone, what remains is a woman moving through a paradise that has stopped explaining itself, and an attention held on her well past the point of innocence. Desire and dread come off the same frames. Almost nothing was added; the whole procedure is removal and rearrangement, performed on footage shot by other people for other purposes in another decade. The National Film Registry holds it, filed among films whose makers owned what they photographed. Twenty minutes is enough to make that ownership look like a technicality.

A bear takes a series of odd jobs to buy his aunt a present, and then the present is stolen. That is the entire engine of a hundred and four minutes, and the restraint is the interesting part: nothing cosmic is at stake, only a debt of gratitude and the small labour of settling it. Paul King stages slapstick that requires every person in the frame to be sincere, which is far harder to sustain than irony and ages better. The Guardian placed it among the hundred best films of the century, in company that is difficult on purpose; it holds the seat by being exact rather than by being sweet. Timing, courtesy and consequence are the materials. The politeness is not decoration here, it is the mechanism, and the jokes land because the bear means every word.

Two temperaments, one rented house, one summer: she is a professor and precise about it, he paints in something close to ecstasy. The city that had been holding the balance between them is somewhere behind them now. Kathleen Collins hands the harder position to the wife, since being the one who thinks, in a marriage where the other person feels loudly, means always sounding like the obstacle. Eighty-six minutes, listed as comedy as much as drama, and the comedy is genuine: the film is amused by both of them and lets neither win an argument on temperament alone. What it takes seriously is her curiosity, which belongs to her and not to the marriage. The National Film Registry has it. The summer is no metaphor, only a house, a stretch of time off, and two people learning how much of the marriage was the city.

The plan is stated without embarrassment: marry a Brazilian millionaire. Everything charming about Holly Golightly is in service of that plan, and Blake Edwards lets the charm run at full strength while never quite concealing the arithmetic beneath it, the rent and the wardrobe and the cost of an evening in New York in 1961. Then a young writer moves into the building, one floor away, observant. A hundred and fifteen minutes shot as romantic comedy and built like a study of a woman managing her own solvency, with a past that has not agreed to stay past. What keeps it from curdling is that the film likes her without needing her to be honest. Nearly everyone knows the images from this one. Fewer have sat with how much bookkeeping goes on inside it, or how close the comedy runs to a colder story.

Twenty-two years old, on a factory wage, with two days out of seven that belong to him, and he spends them as if the arithmetic could be argued with. Karel Reisz keeps ninety minutes at the level of that wage: the shop floor, the pub, a rented room, and an older married woman whose situation is not a plot device but a fact with a household attached. The drinking and the brawling are neither liberation nor squalor here; they are what the money is for. What the film understands is that a young man with a full pay packet on Saturday is a different person from the same man on Monday, and that only one of the two gets to make decisions. It sits in the BFI's hundred British films, and it reads less as a period document than as a wage with a face on it.
